The Rock grenadier (Coryphaenoides rupestris) is a benthopelagic macrourid that exhibits remarkable longevity, with the oldest documented individuals surviving up to 19,710 days [am = up to 19,710 days] under the cold thermal conditions of 8 °C [T = 8 °C] characteristic of its deep-sea habitat. This profound lifespan positions the species among the more long-lived members of the Macrouridae family and reflects the slow metabolic pace typical of abyssal teleosts. Field surveys employing otolith microchemistry have confirmed that somatic growth continues throughout most of this extended life, although at a progressively decelerating rate as individuals approach their maximum recorded total length of 110 centimeters [Li = 110 centimeters]. Such a large ultimate body size is unusual among grenadiers inhabiting the North Atlantic, where most congeneric species plateau at considerably smaller dimensions. The combination of extreme longevity and substantial terminal length suggests a life-history strategy heavily weighted toward the accumulation of somatic tissue before the onset of reproductive investment, an interpretation consistent with the energetic constraints imposed by the region's chronically low temperatures and limited trophic resources.

Sexual maturation in Coryphaenoides rupestris is a protracted process, with individuals typically attaining puberty at a total length of 52.7 centimeters [Lp = 52.7 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to roughly half the species' ultimate length. This intermediate size at maturity indicates that a considerable fraction of the lifespan is devoted to a purely somatic phase before gametogenesis commences. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from specimens collected along the continental slope of the mid-Atlantic Ridge reveals that the transition from an immature to a reproductively competent state is accompanied by a marked increase in vitellogenic oocyte diameter, though the precise age at which this pubertal milestone is reached exhibits substantial inter-individual variation linked to local food availability. The length-based nature of this maturational trigger, rather than an age-based one, is a recurring pattern among deep-water gadiforms and is thought to reflect the unpredictability of encountering sufficient prey biomass to sustain the elevated energetic demands of ovarian development. Once this pubertal length is achieved, the fish enter a phase of iteroparous reproduction that may extend for several decades.

Female Rock grenadier produce large, yolky pelagic eggs whose small dimensions nonetheless impose constraints on neonatal energetics. Based on an average egg diameter of 2.6 millimeters, the calculated wet weight at birth is approximately 0.0092 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0092 grams], a value that places the newly hatched yolk-sac larva among the smallest of macrourid offspring. This exceedingly low initial body mass necessitates a rapid transition to exogenous feeding after yolk-sac resorption, as the endogenous reserves are insufficient to sustain prolonged endotrophic development. The hatchling's minute size also renders it particularly vulnerable to starvation during the critical first-feeding period, a bottleneck that likely exerts strong selective pressure on the timing and location of spawning events to coincide with peaks in planktonic prey availability. Field sampling of ichthyoplankton in the Irminger Sea has confirmed that the free-swimming prolarvae are virtually transparent and possess a poorly developed mouth gape at eclosion, further underscoring the precarious energetic position of the newly emerged individual. The 0.0092 gram [Wwb = 0.0092 gram] mass at hatching represents an extreme point in the species' ontogenetic trajectory of weight gain.

The maximum reproductive rate documented for this species, estimated under the cold thermal regime of 8 °C [T = 8 °C] that prevails throughout its bathymetric range, corresponds to a daily output of approximately 188 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 188 eggs per day]. This fecundity value has been derived from counts of hydrated oocytes in gravid females captured during the peak spawning season and reflects the species' strategy of producing numerous small eggs rather than a smaller number of large, well-provisioned ones. The annual reproductive output is therefore enormous, with a single female capable of shedding many tens of thousands of eggs over the course of a protracted spawning period. Such high fecundity is a common adaptation among deep-sea teleosts, offsetting the extraordinarily high larval mortality rates that prevail in the oligotrophic waters of the North Atlantic. Importantly, this daily egg production rate has only been observed in populations inhabiting waters at 8 °C, and it remains unclear whether females living at the warmer periphery of the species' distribution exhibit comparable levels of ovarian investment, as temperature-mediated metabolic scaling may impose different constraints on egg production.

The ultimate wet weight attained by Coryphaenoides rupestris adults reaches approximately 1700 grams [Wwi = approximately 1700 grams], a value that places the species among the heavier macrourids in the North Atlantic assemblage. This substantial terminal mass is achieved only after decades of continuous growth, with the largest individuals—those exceeding 100 centimeters in total length—concentrated in the oldest age classes. The transition from a 0.0092 gram neonate to the 1700 gram adult represents an increase in body mass of over five orders of magnitude, a trajectory that is mediated by the gradual accumulation of both skeletal and soft tissues across the lengthy lifespan. At the prevailing environmental temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C], the metabolic costs of somatic maintenance are relatively low, permitting the sustained allocation of assimilated energy toward growth throughout the majority of the life cycle before senescence eventually imposes a physiological ceiling on further mass gain.
